newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: U.N. envoy in last-ditch Afghan peace bid.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy in last-ditch Afghan peace bid.

text.p: A United Nations envoy is scheduled to arrive in this Afghan rebel headquarters on Thursday in a last-ditch effort to head off a bloody battle for the Afghan capital Kabul.

With rebel troops less than 10 miles (16 km) from Kabul, within easy rocket and artillery range, envoy Norbert Holl's mission was regarded as a final chance to avert a new cycle of violence that some analysts believe could lead to a de facto partition of Afghanistan.

The possible battle for the capital pits the Taleban, an Islamic fundamentalist movement of mainly southern Afghan Pashtuns who control Kabul, against a less fundamentalist alliance of ethnic Uzbeks, Tajiks and Hazaras controlling the northern part of the country.

The main leaders of the alliance are Tajik frontline commander Ahmed Shah Masood, a hero of the battle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan, and General Malik Pahlwan, an enigmatic 37-year-old Uzbek warlord based in this northern Afghan town, from where the alliance has launched bombing raids on Kabul in recent days.
Malik was expected to take part in the talks with Holl while Masood would be represented by aides because he could not leave the tense front lines, where his presence is regarded as key to victory.

Holl's mission, described by U.N. sources in Mazar-i-Sharif as a fact-finding tour, aims to lay the groundwork for a visit in about one week's time by U.N. Secretary-General Koffi Annan's newly-appointed envoy for Afghanistan, Lakhdar Brahimi, a former Algerian Foreign Minister and former U.N. envoy to Haiti.

But in this headquarters of the northern alliance, rebel officials and foreign aid workers questioned whether, with alliance forces virtually at the gates of Kabul, time had already run out for peace talks.

General Malik told reporters on Wednesday the basis of the U.N. talks should be the immediate demilitarisation of Kabul followed by negotiations between the warring parties in one of three nations which have offered to host talks.
"We support U.N. efforts to save the people of Kabul. We are ready to travel to any of those countries -- Italy, Japan, Kyrgyzstan -- for talks if there is demilitarisation of Kabul," Malik said.
He urged the United Nations to take an active role in demilitarising Kabul, hinting that the capital should be controlled by a multinational U.N. force while negotiations went on for a solution.

U.N. sources in Mazar-i-Sharif told Reuters that in verbal contacts with alliance officials, the rebels had suggested that their forces and Taleban fighters should withdraw out of rocket range of the capital -- about 40 km (25 miles) -- as part of a demilitarisation plan, leaving the capital's security to the proposed U.N. multinational force.
"They talk about 1,000 or 2,000 blue helmets running the city," one U.N. source said.

However the sources said because of the world organisation's budget problems and donor fatigue over Afghanistan, it would take too long, up to six months, to put together a multinational force, even if there were international will to do so.
"Things are not going to wait nearly that long," a U.N. source on the spot said.
Another alternative, to put together an Afghan force acceptable to both sides, was regarded as completely impossible because of the distrust between the Afghan ethnic groups and warlords.

U.N. sources said alliance officials were telling them that Taleban forces already believed their position was hopeless in holding Kabul, and some renegade Taleban groups had already started looting the city ahead of a withdrawal from the capital towards areas they control near the Pakistan border.
"Alliance officials are warning of an imminent popular uprising against the Taleban in Kabul," a U.N. source said.
"They say that if this happens Alliance forces will have to enter Kabul to restore order," the source said. "Our mission is a race against time."

There was no word on whether either Holl or the new U.N. envoy would meet the leaders of the Taleban, who have refused to join peace talks until thousands of prisoners held by the Alliance in three locations around Mazar-i-Sharif are released.
